Complementary information — The documents provide non‑contradictory details on value, rarity, and specific gemstone types.

The evidence clusters by gemstone type and nuance: d2, d4, and d6 state unheated stones are generally more valuable and rarer [d2, d4, d6]. d1, d3, and d8 add conditional specifics—value depends on identical quality [d1], shows price differences for rubies [d3], and quantifies value loss for specific stones [d8]. d9 notes rarity of unheated stones. These facets complement each other without contradiction.

The complementary snippets together show that heated gemstones are typically less valuable than unheated ones, primarily due to rarity and consumer preference for natural stones. However, the degree and conditions vary by gem type, quality comparison, and market.

Heated gemstones are generally less valuable than unheated ones because unheated stones are rarer and more desirable [d2, d4, d6]. For example, unheated sapphires and rubies command higher prices [d2, d6], and heating can cause ruby and sapphire to lose about half their value compared to unheated equivalents [d8]. The value difference is clearest when comparing stones of otherwise identical quality [d1], and specific price examples for rubies show unheated stones are valued higher per carat [d3]. Unheated natural gemstones are very rare in the market [d9], which supports their premium.
